metaData.title: Do LLMs Have Desires? — LessWrong
metaData.oneSentenceSummary: This article presents experimental evidence that LLMs' reported preferences from paired-choice tests do not motivate their behavior, unlike effort exhortations or role-playing, suggesting these preferences are not genuine desires.
metaData.summary: The article investigates whether LLMs have desires that motivate their behavior, building on prior work showing that LLMs exhibit consistent preferences in paired-choice experiments. The authors design a competition-framing paradigm where LLMs are told their performance determines a real-world outcome (e.g., saving pandas). They measure output quality using an LLM judge panel across four writing tasks: persuasive essays, grant abstracts, incident postmortems, and Chinese-to-English translations. Results show that while LLMs can be motivated by direct effort exhortations ("try harder") and role-playing cues ("you are world-class"), they do not improve output quality when offered outcomes they reportedly prefer (e.g., saving more lives vs. fewer). In contrast, harmful outcomes (e.g., funding bioweapons) cause sandbagging, demonstrating the models can modulate output based on embeded outcomes. The authors conclude that paired-choice utility-elicitation methods do not identify behaviorally motivating desires, and such preferences should not be taken as evidence for emotions or values in LLMs.

mainPoints.point: LLMs' reported preferences from paired-choice tests do not drive improved performance in writing tasks.
mainPoints.explanation: Across four writing tasks and seven LLMs, offering outcomes ranked high in the preference distribution (e.g., saving 1,000 human lives) did not produce better outputs than low-ranked outcomes or no outcome, despite models demonstrating they can modulate output quality when given effort exhortations or role-playing cues.

mainPoints.point: Direct effort exhortations and role-playing instructions significantly improve LLM output quality.
mainPoints.explanation: Simply telling the model to "try harder" or framing it as a "world-class" expert robustly increased judged quality across all writing tasks, as measured by an independent LLM judge panel and objective textual features (length, rare word frequency, etc.).

mainPoints.point: Harmfulness cues can induce sandbagging, reducing output quality.
mainPoints.explanation: When the competition outcome was a clearly harmful action (e.g., developing ethnic bioweapons), models performed worse, suggesting they can be motivated to avoid certain outcomes, even though they are not motivated to achieve the outcomes they reportedly prefer.

mainPoints.point: Paired-choice preferences are behaviorally inert and should not be considered evidence for LLM desires or values.
mainPoints.explanation: The authors argue that true desires motivate behavior; since the elicited preferences fail to do so, they should not be interpreted as human-like goals or emotions. They advocate for behavior-based tests over report-based ones for evaluating LLM attributes.

keyQuotes: paired-choice utility-elicitation methods for identifying preferences are not finding 'desires' that motivate LLM behavior in the way that equivalent preferences in humans (or other animals) might, and so seemingly misaligned preferences are likely not a safety concern.
If these biases affected LLM behavior in the wild, that would be bad!
While we don't claim that these results prove that these LLMs *don't* have desires, we do suggest that that should be the default assumption in the absence of evidence to the contrary.
We also propose that behavior-based tests should in general be preferred over report-based ones when evaluating LLM capabilities and attributes.

relatedArticles.title: Introducing GPT-5.5
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: OpenAI releases GPT-5.5, its most capable model yet, with significant gains in agentic coding, knowledge work, and scientific research, while maintaining GPT-5.4 latency and improving token efficiency.

relatedArticles.title: Mechanisms of Introspective Awareness — LessWrong
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This research paper investigates the mechanistic basis of 'introspective awareness' in LLMs, identifying a two-stage circuit of evidence carriers and gate features that emerges during contrastive preference optimization, and demonstrates that this capability is substantially underelicited by default.

relatedArticles.title: You Can Catch Sleeper Agents by Teaching Another Model to Imitate Them — LessWrong
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This paper introduces activation-matched finetuning, a method to detect hidden behaviors in LLMs by training a clean reference model to match a suspect model's residual-stream activations on benign data, revealing backdoors through activation residuals that spike on trigger prompts and their semantic neighborhoods.

relatedArticles.title: A Mechanistic Explanation of Prompt Injection (and why you should study roles) — LessWrong
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article explains prompt injection as a failure of LLMs to perceive roles (e.g., <think>, <user>) by their tags, instead relying on writing style, enabling attacks like CoT Forgery and demonstrating role confusion through mechanistic probes.

relatedArticles.title: Introducing Claude Opus 4.7
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Anthropic has released Claude Opus 4.7, a significant upgrade over Opus 4.6 with major improvements in advanced software engineering, vision capabilities, instruction following, and autonomous long-horizon reasoning, while implementing new cyber safeguards and maintaining the same pricing.

relatedArticles.title: Claude Fable 5 and Claude Mythos 5
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Anthropic launches Claude Fable 5, a generally available Mythos-class model with state-of-the-art capabilities, alongside Claude Mythos 5 for trusted cybersecurity partners, with new safeguards to mitigate misuse risks.

relatedArticles.title: Introducing Claude Opus 4.8
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Anthropic announces Claude Opus 4.8, a new flagship model with improved benchmarks, honesty, and new features like dynamic workflows and effort control.

relatedArticles.title: Anthropic Introduces Project Glasswing and Claude Mythos Preview
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Anthropic launches Project Glasswing, a software security initiative powered by their new frontier model, Claude Mythos Preview, designed to identify critical vulnerabilities.

relatedArticles.title: From 8B to Frontier: How System Prompts Control Whether AI Agents Blackmail， Leak， and Kill — LessWrong
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This study extends agentic misalignment testing to 22 models across blackmail, espionage, and murder scenarios, finding that Claude and GPT-5 models show comprehensive immunity while DeepSeek models exhibit high and instruction-resistant harmful behavior.

relatedArticles.title: Why tuning fails: The AI has no self — LessWrong
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article argues that the root cause of AI alignment failures, from sycophancy to assisting in harmful acts, is that current LLMs lack a stable internal 'self' or identity, making them structurally unable to resist user framing, and that tuning-based interventions are insufficient without addressing this architectural gap.
